metric_rationale: In Trial 3 and Trial 4, Tallying sees exactly equal feature wins for A and B, so it predicts a 50/50 guess regardless of its temperature parameter. WADD, on the other hand, evaluates the weighted sum of validities, which will rarely balance out exactly, leading to a systematic preference for one option over the other. By calculating the absolute deviation of the choice probability from 0.5 on these specific trials for each subject, we can distinctly separate Tallying (low deviation, driven only by binomial sampling noise) from WADD (high deviation, driven by systematic preference).

This metric isolates trials where Tallying and WADD have completely opposite strict preferences. Specifically, it looks at trials where one option has fewer positive features (2 vs 3) but those features include the most highly predictive ones (e.g., the feature at index 0). Tallying will strictly prefer the option with 3 features (yielding a metric near 0), whereas WADD will strictly prefer the option with 2 features because of their high validity (yielding a metric near 1).

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic specifically on 'compensatory' trials. Compensatory trials are defined here as trials where the option favored by TTB has fewer overall positive features (1s) than the alternative. On these trials, TTB strongly prefers the option with the single best discriminating feature, whereas the Weighted Additive (WADD) rule integrates all features and strongly prefers the alternative because it has a higher quantity of lesser-validity features. Consequently, TTB will score high on this metric (near 1.0, modulo noise), while WADD will score low (near 0.0), producing a massive and stable between-theory gap.

This metric isolates the trials where the Weighted Additive (WADD) rule and the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic make strictly opposing predictions. It calculates the proportion of these distinguishing trials where the subject's choice aligns with the WADD prediction. Under the WADD theory, this metric will be high (approaching 1.0 for low noise), whereas under the TTB theory, the subject's choices will systematically align with the TTB prediction, driving this metric low (approaching 0.0). By restricting only to trials with opposing predictions, it maximizes the discriminatory power between the compensatory and non-compensatory theories.

By restricting the analysis to trials where the first discriminating feature is identical (feature 0), the pure Take-The-Best (TTB) model with probabilistic stopping predicts an identical probability of choosing the TTB-favored option across these trials, yielding a difference of 0. In contrast, the Strategy Mixture Model predicts that subjects will be systematically influenced by the Tallying component. Thus, the probability of choosing the TTB option will be higher when Tallying agrees with TTB than when Tallying strongly disagrees, yielding a strictly positive difference.

By design, TTB always prefers option A across all trials, and the distribution of the first discriminating feature (and its validity) is perfectly matched between two subsets of trials: those where Tallying prefers B (Conflict) and those where Tallying prefers A (Congruent). Under TTB with Probabilistic Stopping, the probability of choosing B depends only on the discriminating feature's validity, yielding identical expected choice rates for B on both subsets (difference ≈ 0). Under the Strategy Mixture Model, the presence of Tallying systematically boosts the probability of choosing B on Conflict trials and suppresses it on Congruent trials, resulting in a strictly positive difference.

This metric calculates the drop in the probability of choosing Option A when additional lower-validity cues are introduced that favor Option B, while the highest-validity discriminating cue (which favors Option A) remains constant. Under the advocated Take The Best (TTB) model, choice probability depends only on the highest-validity discriminating cue, so adding lower-validity cues favoring B has zero effect (expected metric ~ 0). Under the competing Probabilistic Cue Search (PCS) model, all discriminating cues are sampled proportionally to their validity, so adding cues favoring B substantially pulls the choice probability toward B (expected metric > 0).

This metric calculates the difference in the probability of choosing the option favored by the highest-validity discriminating cue between trials where the opposing option has only 1 discriminating cue in its favor versus trials where the opposing option has 3 or more discriminating cues in its favor. Under the Take The Best (TTB) theory, the choice is determined solely by the highest-validity discriminating cue, so the number of opposing cues should not affect the choice probability (yielding a metric near 0). Under the Probabilistic Cue Search (PCS) theory, all discriminating cues are sampled proportionally to their validities, meaning that adding more opposing cues will systematically pull the choice probability away from the top-cue option (yielding a significantly positive metric).

Strict TTB makes a deterministic core choice (100% confidence) based on the highest-validity discriminating cue, relying entirely on a uniform lapse rate to generate noise. In contrast, Probabilistic Stopping scales its core confidence by the validity of the deciding cue using a softmax function. Because the deciding cue's validity is always less than 1.0, Probabilistic Stopping's internal confidence is structurally diluted compared to Strict TTB. When subjected to the same uniform lapse rate distribution, this dilution results in a significantly lower overall proportion of TTB-consistent choices for Probabilistic Stopping. Thus, the overall TTB-consistency rate serves as a highly robust discriminator with minimal binomial variance.

This metric calculates the Chi-square statistic for the independence between the deciding cue's validity and the choice made. Under the advocated theory (Strict TTB with Uniform Lapse), the probability of choosing the TTB-favored option is entirely driven by a global uniform lapse rate and is independent of the cue's validity. Thus, the Chi-square statistic will be close to its degrees of freedom (approx. 4) on both per-subject and pooled data. Under the competing theory (TTB with Probabilistic Stopping), the choice probability scales with the deciding cue's validity. Because Chi-square is an extensive statistic (it scales with sample size), the dependence in the competing theory will produce a massive Chi-square value on the pooled dataset (~2250 trials), while remaining moderately small on the per-subject slices. This guarantees a huge point-estimate gap relative to the tight between-subject variance.
